name: The Germ Theory of Disease
teaser: Before Pasteur and Koch, doctors thought disease came from 'bad air.' Germ theory proved that microorganisms cause infection — and transformed medicine from superstition into science.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment disproved spontaneous generation, then explain why handwashing took decades to become standard practice.

name: Antibiotics
teaser: Alexander Fleming's accidental discovery of penicillin in 1928 saved more lives than any other drug in history. But overuse is creating superbugs that no antibiotic can kill.

exploreAction.targetName: The story of penicillin and antibiotic resistance
exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Fleming discovered penicillin and how mass production saved soldiers in WWII, then explain why antibiotic resistance is called a 'silent pandemic.'

name: Vaccination
teaser: Edward Jenner's 1796 experiment — cowpox protecting against smallpox — launched immunology. Vaccines have eradicated smallpox, nearly eliminated polio, and saved an estimated 154 million lives in the past 50 years.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between live attenuated, inactivated, subunit, and mRNA vaccines, then explain how herd immunity protects unvaccinated people.

name: DNA and the Double Helix
teaser: Watson and Crick's 1953 discovery of DNA's structure revealed the code of life. But Rosalind Franklin's X-ray crystallography made it possible — and she was denied credit for decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51 and how it revealed the helical structure, then explain why the story of DNA's discovery is also a story about scientific credit.

name: Anaesthesia
teaser: Before 1846, surgery meant screaming. Ether's demonstration at Massachusetts General Hospital — 'Gentlemen, no humbug' — made painless surgery possible and transformed what doctors could do.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the 'Ether Dome' demonstration, then explain how general, regional, and local anaesthesia work differently in the body.

name: X-Rays
teaser: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and immediately took a picture of his wife's hand — the first medical image in history. Within weeks, doctors could see inside living bodies without cutting them open.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Röntgen's discovery and the first X-ray image, then explain how modern CT scans build on the same principle.

name: Blood Types
teaser: Karl Landsteiner discovered that blood transfusions kill people because of incompatible blood types. The ABO system saved millions — and explained why 'universal donor' O-negative matters.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why blood types matter for transfusions and organ donation, then explain why type O-negative is called the 'universal donor.'

name: The Stethoscope
teaser: In 1816, René Laennec rolled a paper tube to listen to a patient's heart — embarrassed to press his ear against her chest. The stethoscope became the symbol of medicine itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Laennec's invention and how auscultation (listening to body sounds) works, then explain why the stethoscope remains essential despite modern imaging.

name: Insulin
teaser: Before 1921, diabetes was a death sentence. Banting and Best's discovery of insulin turned a fatal disease into a manageable condition — and they sold the patent for $1 each.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Banting and Best isolated insulin, then explain why insulin's price controversy matters for millions of diabetics worldwide.

name: Germ Theory and Antisepsis
teaser: Joseph Lister proved that carbolic acid spray during surgery dramatically reduced infection. The 'father of antiseptic surgery' turned operating rooms from death chambers into healing spaces.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Lister's carbolic acid spray technique, then explain why surgical mortality dropped from 45% to 15% after antisepsis was adopted.

name: The Immune System
teaser: Your body's defense network: white blood cells, antibodies, complement, and memory cells fight off billions of invaders daily. When it malfunctions, the results range from allergies to autoimmune disease.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between innate immunity (fast, nonspecific) and adaptive immunity (slow, specific, with memory), then explain why you get chickenpox only once.

name: The Cardiovascular System
teaser: Your heart beats 100,000 times a day, pumping 7,500 liters of blood through 100,000 km of vessels. It's the most reliable pump ever built — and when it fails, everything else follows.

exploreAction.targetName: How the heart and blood vessels work
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the cardiac cycle (systole and diastole), then explain how blood pressure is measured and what the numbers mean.

name: The Nervous System
teaser: 86 billion neurons, each connected to thousands of others: the brain and spinal cord process every sensation, thought, and movement. It's the most complex structure in the known universe.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about action potentials, neurotransmitters, and synapses, then explain how a thought becomes a movement.

name: The Gut Microbiome
teaser: Your gut hosts 38 trillion bacteria — more than your own cells. They digest food, produce vitamins, train your immune system, and may even influence your mood. The microbiome is medicine's newest frontier.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the gut-brain axis and how microbiome diversity affects immunity, then find one dietary change that improves microbiome health.

name: Bone Biology
teaser: Bones aren't dead scaffolding: they're living tissue that constantly remodels. Osteoclasts break down old bone; osteoblasts build new. The skeleton repairs itself daily — until it doesn't.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the bone remodeling cycle, then explain why osteoporosis is called a 'silent disease' and who's most at risk.

name: The Kidneys
teaser: Two fist-sized organs that filter 180 liters of blood daily, producing 1-2 liters of urine. Kidneys regulate blood pressure, balance electrolytes, and produce hormones — yet most people can't name what they do.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about nephrons (the kidney's filtering units), then explain why kidney disease is often called a 'silent killer.'

name: What Is Cancer?
teaser: Cancer is uncontrolled cell growth: cells multiply without stopping, invade nearby tissue, and spread to distant organs. It's not one disease — it's hundreds, each with its own biology and treatment.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about oncogenes, tumor suppressors, and metastasis, then explain why cancer becomes more common with age.

name: Diabetes
teaser: Type 1: the immune system destroys insulin-producing cells. Type 2: the body stops responding to insulin. Both cause blood sugar to rise — and untreated diabetes damages every organ over time.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between Type 1 (autoimmune) and Type 2 (metabolic), then find one lifestyle factor that reduces Type 2 risk.

name: Cardiovascular Disease
teaser: The world's #1 killer: heart disease and stroke account for 17 million deaths annually. Plaque builds in arteries, blood clots form, and the heart or brain loses blood supply.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about atherosclerosis (plaque buildup), then find three modifiable risk factors and one that's genetic.

name: Alzheimer's Disease
teaser: The most common cause of dementia: amyloid plaques and tau tangles destroy brain cells, erasing memory, language, and identity. There's no cure — and the aging global population is making it an epidemic.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about amyloid-beta plaques and tau protein, then explain why early diagnosis is so important and why drug development has been so difficult.

name: Malaria
teaser: A mosquito-borne parasite that kills 600,000 people annually — mostly children in sub-Saharan Africa. Malaria has shaped human evolution, economics, and geography for millennia.

exploreAction.targetName: How malaria parasites evade the immune system
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Plasmodium falciparum's life cycle, then explain why sickle cell trait provides malaria resistance.

name: Antimicrobial Resistance
teaser: Bacteria evolve faster than we can invent new antibiotics. By 2050, drug-resistant infections could kill 10 million people a year — more than cancer. It's the slowest-moving pandemic in history.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about natural selection in bacteria, then find one action individuals can take to slow resistance.

name: Autoimmune Diseases
teaser: When the immune system attacks its own body: lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, type 1 diabetes. There are 80+ autoimmune conditions — and they're increasingly common.

exploreAction.targetName: Why the immune system turns on itself
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about molecular mimicry and loss of self-tolerance, then find one autoimmune condition and its most common symptoms.

name: Depression
teaser: More than sadness: depression is a neurochemical condition affecting 280 million people. It's the leading cause of disability worldwide — and the gap between need and treatment is enormous.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the serotonin hypothesis and its limitations, then explain why depression treatment often combines medication with therapy.

name: Antiviral Drugs
teaser: Viruses hijack your cells to replicate — antivirals stop them at specific steps. HIV antiretrovirals turned a death sentence into a chronic condition. Acyclovir treats herpes. Tamiflu shortens flu.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how antivirals target viral replication (entry inhibitors, polymerase inhibitors, protease inhibitors), then find one antiviral that changed public health.

name: Chemotherapy
teaser: Killing cancer cells by poisoning fast-dividing cells — which also kills hair, gut, and bone marrow. Chemotherapy is brutal medicine, but it's saved millions of lives since the 1940s.

exploreAction.targetName: How chemotherapy works and its side effects
exploreAction.instruction: Learn why chemotherapy targets fast-dividing cells, then explain why newer targeted therapies cause fewer side effects.

name: Organ Transplantation
teaser: Replacing a failed organ with one from a donor: kidney, liver, heart, lung. The surgery is miraculous; the waiting list is heartbreaking. Immunosuppression keeps the body from rejecting the gift.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about tissue matching, immunosuppression, and organ donation systems, then explain why xenotransplantation (animal-to-human) is being pursued.

name: MRI Imaging
teaser: Magnetic resonance imaging uses powerful magnets and radio waves to see inside the body without radiation. It can distinguish gray matter from white, tumor from healthy tissue — the most detailed medical images available.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about hydrogen atoms in magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses, then explain why MRI is better than CT for soft tissue imaging.

name: CT Scanning
teaser: Computed tomography: X-rays from hundreds of angles, reconstructed by computer into 3D slices of the body. CT scans diagnose strokes, cancers, and trauma in minutes — but expose patients to radiation.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Radon transform and how CT reconstruction works, then explain why CT is preferred for trauma and MRI for neurological conditions.

name: Physical Therapy
teaser: Restoring movement after injury, surgery, or stroke: physical therapists use exercise, manual therapy, and education to help bodies heal themselves. It's medicine without drugs.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about therapeutic exercise principles (progressive overload, specificity), then find one condition where physical therapy is first-line treatment.

name: Clinical Trials
teaser: Phase I (safety), Phase II (efficacy), Phase III (comparison), Phase IV (post-market): clinical trials are the gold standard for proving a treatment works. They're slow, expensive, and essential.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the four phases of clinical trials and why randomized controlled trials are the gold standard, then find one drug that failed Phase III trials.

name: The World Health Organization
teaser: The UN's health agency: WHO coordinates global disease surveillance, sets health standards, and responds to pandemics. Its successes (smallpox eradication) and failures (COVID response) reshape global health.

exploreAction.targetName: What WHO does and how it's funded
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about WHO's core functions and funding structure, then evaluate its COVID-19 response.

name: The Hippocratic Oath
teaser: 'First, do no harm': the ancient Greek oath that defines medical ethics. Modern versions focus on patient autonomy, confidentiality, and justice — but the core principle remains: the patient comes first.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hippocratic Oath and medical ethics
exploreAction.instruction: Read both the original Hippocratic Oath and a modern version (Declaration of Geneva), then compare their priorities.

name: Public Health
teaser: Not treating individual patients — but preventing disease in populations. Sanitation, vaccination, clean water, tobacco regulation: public health has saved more lives than all hospitals combined.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the CDC's 'Ten Great Public Health Achievements,' then find one public health intervention that's underfunded today.

name: Evidence-Based Medicine
teaser: Decisions based on the best available research, not tradition or intuition. EBM transformed medicine in the 1990s — but critics argue it can ignore individual patient needs.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about systematic reviews and meta-analyses, then explain why EBM sometimes conflicts with clinical experience.

name: Precision Medicine
teaser: Treating patients based on their genes, not just their symptoms: pharmacogenomics, targeted therapies, and personalized risk profiles. The future of medicine is tailored to you.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about pharmacogenomics (how genes affect drug response), then find one example where genetic testing changes treatment decisions.

name: Telemedicine
teaser: Doctor visits via video call: telemedicine exploded during COVID-19 and isn't going back. It improves access for rural patients but raises questions about physical examination and digital divides.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the advantages and limitations of telemedicine, then find one telehealth service that's improving access in underserved areas.

name: The Surgeon General's Warning
teaser: In 1964, Surgeon General Luther Terry released the first report linking smoking to cancer. The tobacco industry fought it for decades — but the report saved millions of lives through regulation and awareness.

exploreAction.targetName: How the tobacco report changed public health
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the 1964 Surgeon General's report and the tobacco industry's response, then explain why it's a model for evidence-based policy.

name: Florence Nightingale
teaser: The 'Lady with the Lamp' who revolutionized nursing: Nightingale used statistics to prove that sanitation saved lives. Her polar area diagrams were among the first infographics — and they changed hospital design forever.

exploreAction.targetName: How Nightingale used statistics to save lives
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Nightingale's Coxcomb diagrams and her Crimean War statistics, then explain why she's considered the founder of modern nursing.

name: Jonas Salk
teaser: The man who cured polio: Salk's inactivated polio vaccine (1955) was one of medicine's greatest triumphs. He famously refused to patent it — 'Could you patent the sun?'

exploreAction.targetName: Salk vs Sabin: the polio vaccine debate
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Salk's killed vaccine vs Sabin's oral vaccine, then explain why most countries now use Salk's approach.

name: Louis Pasteur
teaser: The chemist who proved germs cause disease, invented pasteurization, and developed vaccines for rabies and anthrax. Pasteur bridged chemistry and medicine — and his name is everywhere (pasteurized milk).

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the swan-neck flask experiment, pasteurization, and the rabies vaccine, then explain why Pasteur is considered the father of microbiology.

name: William Osler
teaser: The 'Father of Modern Medicine': Osler brought medical students to the bedside, insisted on observation over theory, and wrote The Principles and Practice of Medicine. His teaching methods are still used today.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Osler's clinical teaching methods, then explain why he insisted that 'the best teaching is that taught by the patient.'

name: COVID-19
teaser: The pandemic that changed everything: SARS-CoV-2 killed millions, overwhelmed health systems, and accelerated vaccine technology by a decade. mRNA vaccines were developed in record time.

exploreAction.targetName: How mRNA vaccines were developed so fast
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the mRNA technology platform that enabled rapid vaccine development, then explain why mRNA vaccines represent a paradigm shift in immunology.

name: Radiation Therapy
teaser: Using radiation to kill cancer cells: targeted beams destroy DNA in tumors. Modern techniques (IMRT, proton therapy) can hit tumors with millimeter precision while sparing healthy tissue.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between external beam radiation and brachytherapy, then explain why fractionated dosing (small doses over weeks) is more effective than one big dose.

name: Prosthetics
teaser: From wooden legs to mind-controlled bionic limbs: prosthetics engineering has gone from replacement to enhancement. Osseointegration and neural interfaces are blurring the line between human and machine.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about myoelectric prosthetics and osseointegration, then find one breakthrough in bionic limbs that's changing lives.

name: Palliative Care
teaser: Not giving up — giving comfort: palliative care manages pain, symptoms, and quality of life for seriously ill patients. It's not just for the dying; it improves outcomes for the living too.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between palliative care and hospice, then explain why palliative care is increasingly offered alongside curative treatment.

name: Genetic Testing
teaser: From 23andMe to BRCA testing: genetic tests can predict disease risk, guide treatment, and reveal ancestry. But the results raise questions about privacy, insurance, and psychological burden.

exploreAction.targetName: The promises and pitfalls of genetic testing
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about BRCA testing for breast cancer risk, then debate whether genetic information should be shared with insurance companies.

name: Surgical Sterile Technique
teaser: Scrubbing, gowning, gloving, draping: surgical sterile technique is a ritual of infection prevention. Every step exists because someone, somewhere, died when it was skipped.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the principles of surgical asepsis, then explain how a single breach in technique can cause a surgical site infection.

name: Fecal Microbiota Transplant
teaser: Transplanting gut bacteria from a healthy donor to treat infection: FMT has a 90% success rate for C. difficile. It's proof that your microbiome isn't just along for the ride — it's essential medicine.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about C. difficile infection and how FMT restores healthy gut bacteria, then explain why the FDA treats FMT as a drug.

name: Cancer Immunotherapy
teaser: Teaching the immune system to fight cancer: checkpoint inhibitors, CAR-T cells, and cancer vaccines are producing remissions where chemotherapy failed. It's the biggest oncology breakthrough in decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors and CAR-T cell therapy, then explain why immunotherapy can cause autoimmune side effects.

name: Medical Journals
teaser: The Lancet, NEJM, BMJ: medical journals are where discoveries are announced, debated, and scrutinized. Peer review isn't perfect — but it's the best system we have for separating good science from bad.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about peer review, preprints, and the replication crisis in medical research, then find one landmark paper that changed medical practice.

name: Reproductive Biology
teaser: From ovulation to implantation: the human reproductive system is a precision-timed cascade of hormones, cells, and signals. Understanding it has transformed fertility, contraception, and women's health.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, then explain how hormonal contraceptives work by disrupting this cycle.

name: Stem Cell Research
teaser: Cells that can become any tissue: stem cells hold the promise of regenerating damaged organs, curing spinal injuries, and growing replacement tissue. The science is powerful; the ethics are complicated.

exploreAction.targetName: Types of stem cells and their potential
exploreAction.instruction: Learn the difference between embryonic and adult stem cells, then find one clinical trial using stem cells and its current status.

name: Epidemiology
teaser: The detective work of public health: tracking disease patterns, identifying risk factors, and determining causes. Epidemiology found the link between smoking and cancer — and between COVID and lungs.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about cohort studies, case-control studies, and relative risk, then find one epidemiological study that changed public health policy.

name: Tropical Medicine
teaser: Diseases of poverty and heat: malaria, dengue, schistosomiasis, leishmaniasis. Tropical medicine was born in colonial empires and now serves the 3 billion people in equatorial regions.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the WHO's list of neglected tropical diseases, then explain why they persist despite being treatable.

name: Neuroplasticity
teaser: The brain rewires itself after injury, practice, and experience. Stroke patients relearn walking; London taxi drivers grow hippocampi. Neuroplasticity is why rehabilitation works — and why habits are so hard to break.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about London taxi driver studies and stroke rehabilitation, then explain why neuroplasticity declines with age.

name: Chronopharmacology
teaser: When you take a drug matters as much as which drug you take: blood pressure medication works better at night; statins are more effective in the evening. Your body clock affects drug metabolism.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about circadian rhythms and drug metabolism, then find one medication where timing significantly affects its efficacy.

name: Pandemic Preparedness
teaser: COVID-19 proved that pandemics aren't black swans — they're predictable. Stockpiles, surveillance systems, vaccine platforms, and international coordination are the tools that will save us next time.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about strategic national stockpiles and disease surveillance networks, then find one lesson from COVID that's being applied to future preparedness.

name: The Eradication of Smallpox
teaser: Smallpox killed 300 million people in the 20th century alone. The WHO's global vaccination campaign eradicated it in 1980 — the only human disease ever completely wiped out by deliberate effort.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the ring vaccination strategy that finally eradicated smallpox, then find one lesson from that campaign being applied to polio eradication today.

name: mRNA Vaccines
teaser: Instead of injecting a weakened virus, mRNA vaccines teach your cells to build a viral protein themselves — your immune system then learns to recognise it. Katalin Kariko and Drew Weissman spent 20 years perfecting it before COVID made it urgent.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about lipid nanoparticle delivery of mRNA, then find one disease beyond COVID where mRNA vaccines are now in clinical trials.

name: CRISPR Gene Editing
teaser: CRISPR-Cas9 lets scientists cut DNA at precise locations like molecular scissors — adapted from a bacterial immune system, it won the 2020 Nobel Prize and has already cured sickle cell disease in clinical trials.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how CRISPR-Cas9 works as a bacterial immune defence, then find one ethical debate about using it on human embryos.

name: The Human Genome Project
teaser: A 13-year international effort that mapped all 3 billion base pairs of human DNA — completed in 2003, it cost $2.7 billion and revolutionised medicine. Today a whole genome can be sequenced for $200.

exploreAction.targetName: The Human Genome Project and its impact
exploreAction.instruction: Learn what the Human Genome Project discovered, then find one medical breakthrough that was only possible because of it.

name: William Harvey and Blood Circulation
teaser: In 1628 Harvey proved that blood circulates through the body in a loop — overturning 1,400 years of Galen's theory that blood was made in the liver and consumed by the organs.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Harvey's quantitative approach — he calculated blood volume to prove circulation — then find one consequence of getting circulation wrong.

name: Aspirin
teaser: Willow bark was used as pain relief for 4,000 years before chemists isolated salicylic acid in 1897 and buffered it to stop stomach irritation. Aspirin remains the most widely used drug on Earth — over 100 billion tablets per year.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the 4,000-year journey from willow bark to acetylsalicylic acid, then find one surprising modern use for aspirin beyond pain relief.

name: The Lymphatic System
teaser: A parallel circulatory network of vessels and nodes that drains fluid from tissues and fights infection — it has no pump of its own, relying on muscle movement and gravity. When it fails, limbs swell to enormous size.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how lymph nodes filter pathogens, then find one condition caused by a blocked lymphatic system.

name: The Endocrine System
teaser: Hormones are the body's slow messaging system — released into the bloodstream by glands, they regulate metabolism, growth, mood, and reproduction. The thyroid alone controls how fast every cell in your body burns energy.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the hypothalamus–pituitary axis, then find one disease caused by hormone imbalance that most people have heard of.

name: The Liver
teaser: The liver performs over 500 functions — it detoxifies blood, produces bile, stores glucose, and can regenerate from as little as 25% of its original mass. It's the only internal organ with this power.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about liver regeneration, then find one lifestyle factor that damages the liver faster than it can repair itself.

name: The Respiratory System
teaser: Your lungs contain 480 million alveoli — tiny air sacs with a combined surface area of 70 m², roughly the size of a tennis court, all folded inside your chest. Every breath exchanges gases across a membrane just one cell thick.

exploreAction.targetName: How gas exchange works in the lungs
exploreAction.instruction: Learn how oxygen crosses the alveolar membrane, then find one lung disease that destroys alveoli and explain how it limits breathing.

name: The Skin
teaser: Your skin is your largest organ — 1.7 m² of barrier tissue that sheds 30,000–40,000 dead cells every hour. It has its own immune cells, sensory neurons, and microbiome. You replace your entire outer layer every 2–3 weeks.

exploreAction.targetName: The skin as an immune organ
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Langerhans cells in the skin, then find one way the skin microbiome protects against infection.

name: The Eye and Vision
teaser: The human eye can distinguish about 10 million colours but only 5 million of those are differentiable. The retina has 6 million cones and 120 million rods — your peripheral vision is almost entirely black-and-white.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about rod and cone cells, then find one reason colour-blind people see the world differently than you think.

name: The Ear and Hearing
teaser: The smallest bones in your body are in your ear — the stapes is just 3 mm long. Hair cells in the cochlea convert vibrations into electrical signals at frequencies from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Once damaged, they never regenerate.

exploreAction.targetName: How the ear converts sound to signal
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about cochlear hair cells, then find one everyday noise level that can permanently damage them.

name: Pain Science
teaser: Pain is not a simple signal from injury to brain — it's constructed by the brain based on context, expectation, and emotion. Phantom limb pain proves this: people feel excruciating pain in limbs that no longer exist.

exploreAction.targetName: How pain is created in the brain
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the gate control theory of pain, then find one example where expectation changed how much pain someone felt.

name: Migraine
teaser: A migraine is not a bad headache — it's a neurological event involving cortical spreading depression, a wave of brain activity that sweeps across the visual cortex causing aura, followed by hours of throbbing pain, nausea, and light sensitivity.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about cortical spreading depression, then find one new class of migraine drugs that targets the CGRP pathway.

name: Influenza
teaser: The flu kills 290,000–650,000 people every year. The virus mutates so rapidly that last year's vaccine barely recognises this year's strain — that's why you need a new flu shot annually.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about antigenic drift and shift, then find one reason the 1918 flu was so deadly compared to seasonal flu.

name: Tuberculosis
teaser: TB has killed more people than any other infectious disease in history — over 1 billion in the last 200 years alone. Mycobacterium tuberculosis hides inside your own immune cells, and treatment takes 6 months of multiple antibiotics.

exploreAction.targetName: Why TB is so hard to beat
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about granuloma formation, then find one reason antibiotic-resistant TB is a growing global threat.

name: HIV/AIDS
teaser: HIV destroys CD4 T-cells — the coordinators of the immune system — leaving the body vulnerable to infections it would normally fight easily. Antiretroviral therapy turned HIV from a death sentence into a manageable chronic condition.

exploreAction.targetName: How HIV evades the immune system
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about HIV's reverse transcriptase and high mutation rate, then find one case where someone appears naturally resistant to HIV.

name: Cholera and John Snow
teaser: In 1854 John Snow traced a London cholera outbreak to a single water pump — he removed the handle and the epidemic stopped. It was the birth of epidemiology, proving cholera was waterborne before germs were even discovered.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how John Snow mapped cholera cases, then find one modern epidemiological tool that traces disease spread the same way.

name: Ignaz Semmelweis
teaser: In 1847 Semmelweis showed that handwashing in maternity wards cut death rates from 10% to 1%. His colleagues rejected him — he died in an asylum. Germ theory vindicated him 20 years later.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the 'cadaverous particles' hypothesis, then find one reason doctors resisted handwashing despite the data.

name: Alexander Fleming
teaser: Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria in a petri dish he'd left out by accident in 1928 — the discovery of penicillin launched the antibiotic era and has saved an estimated 200 million lives.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the mould Penicillium notatum, then find one reason Fleming warned about antibiotic resistance in his Nobel Prize speech.

name: Rosalind Franklin
teaser: Franklin's X-ray diffraction image 'Photo 51' revealed the helical structure of DNA in 1952 — without her data, Watson and Crick could not have built their model. She died of cancer at 37 and never received the Nobel Prize.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about X-ray crystallography, then find one reason Franklin's contribution was overlooked for decades.

name: Galen
teaser: Galen was the most influential doctor for 1,300 years — his anatomy was wrong in many places (he never dissected humans, only animals), but his authority was so absolute that questioning him was forbidden in universities until the 1600s.

exploreAction.targetName: Why Galen's wrong ideas lasted so long
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Galen's animal-based anatomy, then find one anatomical error he made that persisted for centuries.

name: Ibn Sina (Avicenna)
teaser: Ibn Sina's 'Canon of Medicine' (1025 CE) systematised medical knowledge into a single textbook that was used in European universities until the 1650s — a 600-year standard. He described contagion, quarantine, and over 760 drugs.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Canon of Medicine's structure, then find one medical concept Ibn Sina described 600 years before Europe rediscovered it.

name: The Black Death
teaser: The bubonic plague killed 75–200 million people in the 14th century — up to 60% of Europe's population. It took 200 years for the population to recover, and the labour shortage that followed helped end feudalism.

exploreAction.targetName: How the Black Death changed medicine
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the quarantine concept's origin in Ragusa (1377), then find one lasting change the Black Death caused in European medicine.

name: Bloodletting
teaser: For 2,000 years doctors believed that removing blood cured disease — George Washington died after losing 2.5 litres of blood in a single day. The practice persisted long after evidence showed it was harmful.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Galen's humoral theory, then find one controlled trial that proved bloodletting does more harm than good.

name: Medical Leeches and Maggots
teaser: Leeches and maggots are FDA-approved medical devices. Leeches relieve venous congestion after reattachment surgery; sterile maggots debride dead tissue from wounds without damaging healthy skin. Medieval medicine was right about something.

exploreAction.targetName: How leeches and maggots are used in modern medicine
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about Hirudo medicinalis in microsurgery, then find one condition where maggot debridement therapy outperforms surgery.

name: Blood Transfusion
teaser: Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood groups in 1901 — before that, transfusions were a deadly gamble. Today over 118 million units of blood are donated worldwide every year, and your donation can be split into red cells, platelets, and plasma.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about blood type compatibility, then find one reason Type O-negative blood is called the universal donor.

name: Organ Donation and Transplantation
teaser: The first successful kidney transplant was in 1954 — the donor was the patient's identical twin, so no immunosuppression was needed. Today over 150,000 organ transplants are performed globally each year, and the waiting list always outnumbers donors.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about tissue matching and immunosuppression, then find one experimental approach to growing transplantable organs in the lab.

name: In Vitro Fertilisation (IVF)
teaser: Louise Brown, born in 1978, was the first IVF baby — her parents had tried for nine years. Today over 10 million IVF babies have been born worldwide. The treatment bypasses blocked fallopian tubes by fertilising eggs outside the body.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the IVF cycle, then find one reason IVF success rates vary by age.

name: The Contraceptive Pill
teaser: Approved in 1960, the pill gave women control over fertility for the first time in history — it's been called the most important invention of the 20th century. Over 100 million women use it today.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about how synthetic hormones suppress ovulation, then find one social change that researchers attribute to the pill's introduction.

name: Gene Therapy
teaser: Gene therapy replaces faulty genes with working copies — in 2023 the first CRISPR-based therapy (Casgevy) was approved for sickle cell disease. It took 30 years of failed attempts before the technique finally worked safely.

exploreAction.targetName: Gene therapy's long road to success
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the Jesse Gelsinger tragedy (1999) and how it set gene therapy back a decade, then find one condition gene therapy can now treat.

name: Sleep Medicine
teaser: Humans spend a third of their lives sleeping — and sleep deprivation increases risk of heart disease, diabetes, and Alzheimer's. During sleep the brain's glymphatic system clears toxic waste proteins, which is why chronic insomnia accelerates cognitive decline.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the glymphatic system, then find one sleep habit that measurably improves cognitive performance.

name: Emergency Medicine
teaser: Emergency medicine didn't exist as a specialty until the 1960s — before that, ERs were run by whoever was available. Today the 'golden hour' principle means trauma survival depends on getting care within 60 minutes of injury.

exploreAction.targetName: The golden hour in trauma care
exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the ATLS (Advanced Trauma Life Support) protocol, then find one innovation that shortened emergency response times.

name: Penicillin Discovery (1928)
teaser: Alexander Fleming noticed mold killing bacteria in a petri dish. The most important accidental discovery in medicine — antibiotics have saved an estimated 200 million lives. Fleming warned about resistance in his Nobel speech.

name: CRISPR Gene Editing (2012)
teaser: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier turned bacterial immune systems into molecular scissors. CRISPR can edit any gene in any organism — curing genetic diseases, creating disease-resistant crops, and raising ethical questions.

name: Vaccination (Jenner, 1796)
teaser: Edward Jenner used cowpox to immunize a boy against smallpox. The technique eradicated smallpox by 1980 and saves 2-3 million lives yearly. Anti-vaccination movements now threaten this progress.

name: DNA Double Helix (1953)
teaser: Watson and Crick built the model of DNA's structure — two sugar-phosphate backbones wound around each other. Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data was crucial. The discovery launched modern genetics.

name: The Human Genome Project (2003)
teaser: Mapped all 3 billion base pairs of human DNA. The $3 billion, 13-year project revealed 20,000-25,000 genes — fewer than expected. It launched personalized medicine and pharmacogenomics.

name: Antiseptic Surgery (Lister, 1867)
teaser: Joseph Lister used carbolic acid to sterilize instruments and wounds, reducing surgical mortality from 45% to 15%. Before antisepsis, surgery killed more people than it saved.

name: Anesthesia (Morton, 1846)
teaser: William Morton publicly demonstrated ether anesthesia at Massachusetts General Hospital. Surgeons stopped using rum and leather straps. The Ether Dome demonstration is the most famous moment in surgical history.

name: The Placebo Effect
teaser: Sugar pills cure real pain. Your brain produces actual morphine when it expects relief. Ted Kaptchuk showed even placebos work better when patients know they are placebos — proving expectation is medicine.

name: Germ Theory (Pasteur, 1860s)
teaser: Louis Pasteur proved microorganisms cause disease — ending centuries of miasma theory. His swan-neck flask experiments, pasteurization, and rabies vaccine transformed medicine from guesswork to science.

name: Organ Transplantation (1954)
teaser: Joseph Murray performed the first successful kidney transplant between identical twins. Today, over 150,000 organ transplants happen yearly — but demand far outstrips supply.

name: The Discovery of Insulin (1921)
teaser: Banting and Best extracted insulin from dog pancreases, turning Type 1 diabetes from a death sentence into a manageable condition. They sold the patent for $1 each — believing insulin should be accessible to all.

name: X-Ray Discovery (Röntgen, 1895)
teaser: Wilhelm Röntgen accidentally discovered X-rays while experimenting with cathode rays. His first image was his wife's hand — she saw her skeleton and exclaimed 'I have seen my death.'

name: The Hippocratic Oath (400 BCE)
teaser: First, do no harm — the medical ethical standard for 2,400 years. Modern versions omit the original ban on surgery and the oath to Apollo. The principle of 'first, do no harm' remains medicine's core promise.

name: MRI Imaging (1977)
teaser: Raymond Damadian built the first MRI scanner, using nuclear magnetic resonance to create detailed body images without radiation. Today, 40 million MRI scans happen yearly — the safest imaging technology.

name: The Discovery of Vitamin C (1932)
teaser: Albert Szent-Györgyi isolated ascorbic acid, explaining why sailors got scurvy. Vitamin C deficiency killed more sailors than storms and battles combined during the Age of Exploration.

name: Stem Cell Research (1998)
teaser: James Thomson derived human embryonic stem cells — capable of becoming any cell type. The discovery promised to cure Parkinson's, diabetes, and spinal cord injuries. It also sparked fierce ethical debates.

name: The Discovery of Blood Types (1901)
teaser: Karl Landsteiner identified the ABO blood group system, explaining why blood transfusions sometimes killed patients. His discovery made safe transfusions possible and saved millions of lives.

name: Microbiology (Leeuwenhoek, 1670s)
teaser: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek built microscopes that revealed bacteria, sperm cells, and blood cells for the first time. He called them 'animalcules.' The invisible world existed before anyone knew.

name: Epidemiology (Snow, 1854)
teaser: John Snow mapped cholera cases in London, proving the Broad Street pump was the source. His work founded epidemiology — the science of disease spread. The map changed public health forever.

name: Antibiotics Resistance (2010s)
teaser: Superbugs — bacteria resistant to all antibiotics — kill 700,000 people yearly. By 2050, drug-resistant infections could kill 10 million annually. The post-antibiotic era threatens to undo a century of progress.

name: The Discovery of H. pylori (1982)
teaser: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren proved stomach ulcers are caused by bacteria, not stress. They drank the bacteria to prove it, winning the Nobel Prize. Medicine ignored their finding for a decade.

name: Deep Brain Stimulation (1997)
teaser: Electrodes implanted in the brain treat Parkinson's tremors, OCD, and depression. The technique opens a new frontier in neuromodulation — electrically tuning the brain's circuits.

name: The Discovery of Platelets (1882)
teaser: Julius Cohnheim identified platelets as blood cells responsible for clotting. The discovery explained why hemophilia patients bleed endlessly — they lack functional platelets.

name: Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy
teaser: MRI's sister technology — measures chemical composition of tissues in real-time. It can detect tumors, monitor metabolism, and measure neurotransmitter levels without surgery.

name: The Discovery of Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP)
teaser: Concentrated blood plasma with growth factors promotes healing. Used by athletes for injuries, by dermatologists for skin rejuvenation, and by dentists for bone regeneration.

name: Immunotherapy for Cancer (2011)
teaser: Checkpoint inhibitors unleash the immune system against cancer. Yervoy and Keytruda turned terminal cancers into manageable diseases for some patients. CAR-T cell therapy engineers immune cells to attack tumors.

name: The Discovery of Radioactivity (Becquerel, 1896)
teaser: Henri Becquerel discovered radioactive emissions from uranium salts. Marie and Pierre Curie isolated polonium and radium, launching nuclear physics and radiation therapy for cancer.

name: CT Scanning (1971)
teaser: Godfrey Hounsfield built the first CT scanner, combining X-rays with computer processing to create cross-sectional body images. It revolutionized diagnosis of brain tumors, strokes, and internal injuries.

name: The Discovery of Prostaglandins (1960s)
teaser: John Vane showed prostaglandins regulate inflammation, leading to aspirin and ibuprofen — the world's most used drugs. He won the Nobel Prize in 1982.

name: Telemedicine (1960s-2020s)
teaser: From NASA monitoring astronauts to pandemic-era video consultations — telemedicine made healthcare accessible remotely. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated adoption by 10 years.

name: The Discovery of Helicobacter pylori (1982)
teaser: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren proved stomach ulcers are caused by bacteria, not stress. They drank the bacteria to prove it, winning the Nobel Prize. Medicine ignored their finding for a decade.

name: mRNA Vaccines
teaser: The technology behind COVID-19 vaccines, using messenger RNA to instruct cells to make spike proteins. Pioneered by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who won the 2023 Nobel Prize. BioNTech and Moderna developed theirs in just 11 months.

name: CRISPR Gene Editing
teaser: A revolutionary tool that allows scientists to cut and edit DNA with precision. Derived from bacterial immune systems, CRISPR-Cas9 was developed by Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier. It earned the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

name: Immunotherapy
teaser: A cancer treatment that harnesses the body's own immune system to fight tumors. CAR-T cell therapy reprograms a patient's T-cells to attack cancer. Checkpoint inhibitors like Keytruda have transformed melanoma survival rates.

name: Microbiome Medicine
teaser: The study of trillions of bacteria living in the human gut and their role in health. The gut contains 100 trillion microorganisms weighing about 2kg. Microbiome transplants have cured Clostridioides difficile infections with 90% success.

name: Telemedicine
teaser: Remote diagnosis and treatment of patients using telecommunications technology. Usage surged 3,800% during COVID-19. Medicare claims for telehealth visits rose from 840,000 in 2019 to 52.7 million in 2020.

name: Antibiotic Resistance
teaser: The growing ability of bacteria to survive drugs designed to kill them. The WHO estimates antimicrobial resistance will cause 10 million deaths annually by 2050. MRSA evolved resistance to methicillin within just two years of its introduction in 1960.

name: Precision Medicine
teaser: Tailoring medical treatment to individual genetic profiles rather than one-size-fits-all approaches. The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003 at a cost of $2.7 billion, made this possible. Tumor profiling now guides cancer therapy selection.

name: Neuroplasticity
teaser: The brain's ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections throughout life. London taxi drivers develop enlarged hippocampi from navigating complex streets. Stroke patients can recover lost functions through targeted rehabilitation.

name: Placebo Effect
teaser: A measurable improvement in health from an inactive treatment simply because the patient believes it will work. Placebo surgeries for knee osteoarthritis performed as well as real operations in a 2002 study. Expectation triggers real dopamine release.

name: Stem Cell Therapy
teaser: Using undifferentiated cells that can develop into any cell type to repair damaged tissues. Induced pluripotent stem cells, created by Shinya Yamanaka in 2006, avoid ethical concerns of embryonic stem cells. Clinical trials treat macular degeneration and spinal cord injuries.

name: Prosthetics Innovation
teaser: Modern artificial limbs with mind-controlled joints and sensory feedback. The LUKE arm, funded by DARPA, allows amputees to feel pressure and temperature. Bionic eyes like the Argus II restore partial vision to retinal disease patients.

name: mRNA Cancer Vaccines
teaser: Personalized vaccines created by sequencing a patient's tumor and designing mRNA to train immune cells against unique mutations. BioNTech's individualized neoantigen therapy showed promising results in pancreatic cancer trials in 2023.

name: AI Diagnostics
teaser: Machine learning algorithms that detect diseases from medical images. Google's DeepMind AI diagnosed diabetic retinopathy with 97% accuracy. AI outperformed radiologists in breast cancer screening by reducing false positives by 5.7% in a 2020 study.

name: Organoids
teaser: Miniature, simplified versions of organs grown from stem cells in laboratories. Brain organoids can develop basic neural circuits. They enable drug testing without human subjects and have modeled Zika virus effects on developing brains.

name: Epigenetics
teaser: Heritable changes in gene expression without altering the DNA sequence itself. Stress, diet, and toxins can modify gene expression through methylation and histone modification. Holocaust survivors' trauma signatures were found in their grandchildren's DNA.

name: Bioprinting
teaser: 3D printing living tissue layer by layer using bioinks loaded with cells. Researchers have printed functional liver tissue, skin grafts, and vascular networks. The ultimate goal is printing transplantable organs to eliminate donor waiting lists.

name: Fecal Microbiota Transplant
teaser: Transferring stool from healthy donors to restore gut bacteria balance. Cures recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection in 90% of cases. The first clinical trial used in the 1950s by Dr. Ben Eiseman at the VA Hospital in Denver.

name: Gene Therapy
teaser: Introducing, altering, or replacing genes within a patient's cells to treat disease. Luxturna, approved in 2017, treats inherited blindness with a single injection. Zolgensma, costing $2.1 million, treats spinal muscular atrophy in infants.

name: Liquid Biopsy
teaser: A simple blood test that detects circulating tumor DNA to find cancer early. It can identify mutations from multiple tumor types simultaneously. Guardant Health's test detects stage I-IV cancers across 50+ tumor types from a single blood draw.

name: Wearable Health Tech
teaser: Smart devices that continuously monitor vital signs like heart rate, blood oxygen, and sleep patterns. The Apple Watch detected irregular heart rhythms in 34% of users in the Apple Heart Study. CGMs now help millions manage diabetes in real time.

name: 3D Printed Organs
teaser: Bioprinting technology that creates living tissue structures layer by layer. Organovo has printed functional liver tissue for drug testing. The first 3D bioprinted human ear, made from patient cells, was implanted in 2022 by 3DBio Therapeutics.

name: Nanomedicine
teaser: Using nanoparticles smaller than 100 nanometers to deliver drugs directly to diseased cells. Lipid nanoparticles carry mRNA vaccines past cell membranes. Nanoparticle-based chemotherapy reduces side effects by targeting only tumor tissue.

name: Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy
teaser: Using controlled doses of psilocybin, MDMA, or ketamine alongside psychotherapy. FDA granted breakthrough therapy designation to psilocybin for depression in 2018. MDMA-assisted therapy reduced PTSD symptoms by 67% in Phase 3 trials.

name: Telestroke Networks
teaser: Video-linked neurologists who diagnose and treat stroke patients in remote hospitals. tPA clot-busting medication must be given within 4.5 hours. Telestroke has expanded access to stroke specialists, cutting treatment times by 30 minutes on average.

name: CAR-T Cell Therapy
teaser: Engineering a patient's own T-cells to recognize and attack cancer by adding a chimeric antigen receptor. Kymriah, approved in 2017, achieved 83% remission in pediatric leukemia patients. A single infusion can cost $475,000.

name: Oncolytic Viruses
teaser: Engineered or natural viruses that selectively infect and destroy cancer cells while sparing healthy tissue. T-VEC, approved in 2015, treats advanced melanoma. Researchers discovered the 1904 case of a leukemia patient whose cancer regressed after influenza infection.

name: Regenerative Medicine
teaser: The field focused on repairing or replacing damaged tissues and organs. Skin grafts from a patient's own cells are now routine. Atala's lab grew a bladder from a patient's cells and implanted it in 2006 — the first lab-grown organ.

name: Companion Diagnostics
teaser: Medical tests that identify which patients will benefit from a specific drug. HER2 testing is required before prescribing Herceptin for breast cancer. These tests are mandatory for 25% of new oncology drug approvals.

name: Digital Therapeutics
teaser: Software-based interventions that deliver evidence-based treatments. Pear Therapeutics' reSET treats substance abuse through cognitive behavioral therapy on smartphones. The FDA cleared the first prescription digital therapeutic in 2017.

name: Hematopoietic Stem Cells
teaser: Blood-forming cells found in bone marrow that regenerate all blood cell types. Bone marrow transplants treat leukemia and lymphoma. Donor matching requires HLA typing — a sibling has a 25% chance of being a perfect match.

name: Pharmacogenomics
teaser: How genes affect a person's response to drugs. CYP450 enzyme variants determine whether patients metabolize medications quickly or slowly. A single CYP2D6 test can predict response to 25% of all prescribed drugs.

name: Antibody-Drug Conjugates
teaser: Targeted cancer therapies that link a chemotherapy drug to a monoclonal antibody, delivering toxic payloads directly to tumor cells. Adcetris, approved in 2011, reduced Hodgkin lymphoma deaths by 75%. They're sometimes called 'guided missiles' of cancer therapy.

name: Islet Cell Transplantation
teaser: Transplanting insulin-producing beta cells from donor pancreases to treat Type 1 diabetes. The Edmonton Protocol, developed in 2000, achieved insulin independence in 80% of recipients at one year. Donor scarcity remains the main limitation.

name: Hypothermia Therapy
teaser: Deliberately lowering body temperature to 32-34°C after cardiac arrest or brain injury. Cooling reduces metabolic demand and protects neurons. Hospitalized cardiac arrest survival rates improved from 26% to 56% with therapeutic hypothermia.

name: Phage Therapy
teaser: Using bacteriophages — viruses that infect bacteria — to treat antibiotic-resistant infections. Pioneered in Georgia in 1920, it fell out of favor in the West after antibiotics emerged. A 2019 case cured a UCSD patient's multi-drug resistant Pseudomonas infection.

name: Gene Drive Technology
teaser: A genetic engineering approach that forces a trait through a population faster than normal inheritance. CRISPR-based gene drives could eliminate malaria-carrying mosquitoes. A trial in Burkina Faso released modified sterile male mosquitoes in 2019.

name: Deep Brain Stimulation
teaser: Implanting electrodes in specific brain regions to treat movement disorders. Approved for Parkinson's disease in 1997, it reduces tremor by 60-90%. Experimental applications treat depression, OCD, and addiction. Targets include the subthalamic nucleus and globus pallidus.

name: Artificial Blood
teaser: Synthetic blood substitutes designed to carry oxygen when donated blood is unavailable. Hemopure, made from bovine hemoglobin, is approved in South Africa. Several US trials failed due to side effects, but research continues for battlefield and emergency use.

name: Tissue Engineering
teaser: Combining cells, scaffolds, and growth factors to build replacement tissues. Integra, a skin substitute, has treated burns since 1985. Researchers engineered a replacement ear using a 3D-printed scaffold seeded with cartilage cells from a patient's rib.

name: Point-of-Care Testing
teaser: Diagnostic tests performed at or near the site of patient care rather than in a laboratory. Glucose meters, pregnancy tests, and rapid COVID tests are examples. Abbott's ID NOW molecular test delivers results in under 15 minutes at the bedside.

name: Optogenetics
teaser: Using light to control neurons that have been genetically modified to express light-sensitive proteins. It allows researchers to turn specific brain circuits on and off with millisecond precision. Karl Deisseroth at Stanford pioneered the technique in 2005.

name: Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy
teaser: Replacing defective mitochondrial DNA by transferring nuclear DNA from the mother's egg into a donor egg. The first baby born with this technique, in Mexico in 2016, had a mother at risk for Leigh syndrome. The UK legalized it in 2015.

name: Molecular Glues
teaser: Small molecules that create new protein-protein interactions, redirecting cellular machinery to destroy disease-causing proteins. Thalidomide, once infamous for birth defects, was discovered to work this way in multiple myeloma. It's now a template for new cancer drugs.

name: Wound Healing Science
teaser: The four-stage process of hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling that repairs tissue. Electroceutical bandages using electrical fields accelerate wound closure by 50%.负压 wound therapy, discovered by Morykwas in 1997, uses vacuum to promote granulation.

name: Ferroptosis
teaser: A recently discovered form of regulated cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation. It differs from apoptosis and necrosis. Scientists are exploring ferroptosis as a way to kill cancer cells that resist traditional chemotherapy.

name: Checkpoint Inhibitors
teaser: Cancer drugs that remove the 'brakes' on immune cells so they can attack tumors. Keytruda, approved in 2014, treats melanoma, lung cancer, and bladder cancer. James Allison and Tasuku Honjo won the 2018 Nobel for discovering PD-1 and CTLA-4 checkpoints.

name: CRISPR Diagnostics
teaser: Using CRISPR gene-editing technology for rapid disease detection. SHERLOCK and DETECTR systems can identify viral RNA in under an hour. They were adapted for COVID-19 testing and can detect Zika, Dengue, and HPV from a single drop of blood.

name: Wearable Insulin Pumps
teaser: Miniature devices that continuously deliver insulin to diabetes patients. The Medtronic 780G automates insulin dosing every five minutes based on glucose readings. Closed-loop systems combine CGMs with pumps to create an artificial pancreas.

name: Xenotransplantation
teaser: Transplanting organs from animals into humans. In January 2022, a genetically modified pig heart was transplanted into David Bennett, who survived two months. porcine kidneys have functioned in brain-dead human recipients for over a month.

name: Fecal Microbiota Pills
teaser: Encapsulated stool samples that restore gut bacteria without a full transplant. Rebyota, approved in 2022, treats recurrent C. difficile. The first pills, called SER-109, were approved in 2023 and showed 70% efficacy in clinical trials.

name: Genetic Testing Prenatal
teaser: Non-invasive prenatal testing analyzing fetal DNA in maternal blood. NIPT can detect Down syndrome with 99% accuracy from a blood draw at 10 weeks. Over 5 million tests have been performed since Panorama launched in 2012.

name: Medical Tricorder
teaser: Handheld diagnostic devices inspired by Star Trek that are becoming real. The Scanadu Scout measured vital signs from a forehead touch. The FDA cleared the first medical tricorder-like device — the AliveCor KardiaMobile — for ECG readings in 2015.

name: Quantum Medicine
teaser: Using quantum mechanics principles for medical diagnostics and treatment. Quantum sensors can detect magnetic fields from neural activity without surgery. Nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamonds are being developed for ultra-sensitive biomagnetic imaging.

name: Tumor Treating Fields
teaser: Alternating electrical fields that disrupt cancer cell division. Optune, approved in 2011 for glioblastoma, uses transducer arrays worn on the scalp. When combined with chemotherapy, it improved median survival from 16 to 21 months.

name: Microbiome Transplants
teaser: Fecal microbiota transplantation replaces unhealthy gut bacteria with healthy ones. C. difficile treatment success rates reached 90% in the first randomized trial in 2013. Researchers are now exploring transplants for obesity, autism, and autoimmune diseases.

name: Robotic Surgery
teaser: Minimally invasive procedures performed by surgeons controlling robotic arms. The da Vinci system, used in over 10 million procedures, provides 3D magnification and wristed instruments with seven degrees of freedom. Recovery times are 50% faster than open surgery.

name: mRNA Therapeutics
teaser: Using messenger RNA to instruct cells to produce therapeutic proteins. Moderna's flu vaccine candidate showed 40% better efficacy than traditional shots in 2023 trials. mRNA therapies for heart disease, autoimmune disorders, and rare genetic diseases are in development.

name: Artificial Pancreas
teaser: Closed-loop insulin delivery systems that automatically adjust dosing based on continuous glucose monitoring. The Medtronic 670G, approved in 2016, was the first hybrid closed-loop system. Users spend 70% more time in target glucose range.

name: Nanobots in Medicine
teaser: Robots at the nanoscale designed for targeted drug delivery and surgery. Rice University's nanobots can drill through cancer cells using molecular motors. MIT researchers built DNA nanobots that can seek out and destroy tumors in animal models.

name: Stem Cell Eyesight
teaser: Using retinal pigment epithelium cells derived from stem cells to treat macular degeneration. The first patient, a Japanese woman, received the therapy in 2014. Clinical trials in the UK showed improved vision in patients with wet age-related macular degeneration.

name: Circadian Medicine
teaser: Timing drug delivery to match the body's internal clock for maximum effectiveness. Chronotherapy for blood pressure medication reduces cardiovascular events by 33% compared to morning dosing. The Nobel Prize in 2017 recognized circadian rhythm research.

name: Bioelectric Medicine
teaser: Using electrical signals to control organ function without drugs. Vagus nerve stimulation treats epilepsy and depression. SetPoint Medical's device reduces inflammation by stimulating the vagus nerve, offering potential treatments for rheumatoid arthritis.

name: Antibiotic Stewardship
teaser: Programs that optimize antibiotic use to combat resistance. Hospital stewardship programs reduce antibiotic use by 30-40% while maintaining outcomes. The WHO declared antibiotic resistance one of the top 10 global public health threats.

name: Implantable Brain Chips
teaser: Neural interfaces that connect the brain to computers. Neuralink's first human implant in January 2024 allowed a paralyzed patient to control a computer cursor with thought. BrainGate's earlier system enabled typing at 90 characters per minute.

name: Glucose Monitoring Implants
teaser: Tiny sensors inserted under the skin that continuously measure blood sugar. The FreeStyle Libre, inserted with a needle in 1 second, provides readings for 14 days. Dexcom G7, approved in 2023, is the most accurate CGM with a mean absolute relative difference of 8.2%.
